title: How does your brain recognize a face?
sources: MIT Department of Brain and Cognitive Sciences

lines.text: In less than one tenth of a second, your brain can spot your best friend in a crowded stadium.
lines.caps: How does your brain *spot | a familiar *face | in 0.1s?

lines.text: Human brains have a dedicated biological supercomputer region called the fusiform face area.
lines.caps: Processed by the *fusiform | face area in | your *brain

lines.text: Instead of scanning features one by one, your brain processes the entire face holistically in parallel.
lines.caps: Scans eyes, nose, and *mouth | all at *once

lines.text: It calculates microscopic spatial distances between pupils, nose tip, and jawline curvature.
It matches this geometric matrix against tens of thousands of stored memory profiles.
This system is so aggressive that it often sees human faces in clouds, electrical outlets, and car grilles.
lines.caps: It's why you see *faces | in toast and car | *grilles!

lines.text: Face recognition is the evolutionary superpower that helped humans survive in social tribes.
